q: What is the maximum recommended duration of a temporary clip?
why: Keep temporary clipping to around 7 minutes; augment BP during it.

q: Why might adenosine be given during aneurysm clipping?
o: To briefly arrest the circulation and soften the aneurysm for clip placement
why: An adenosine bolus (around 0.3–0.6 mg/kg) causes brief asystole; avoid in asthma, coronary disease or conduction problems.

q: The aneurysm ruptures during clipping. What is an appropriate anaesthetic response?
o: Propofol bolus to reduce MAP by 10–20% and CMRO2, while maintaining CPP
why: Reduce MAP modestly and CMRO2 with propofol, communicate with the surgeon, and maintain CPP.

q: What is the transmural pressure across the aneurysm wall?
why: Transmural pressure (and CPP) = MAP − ICP; a sudden fall in ICP (e.g. dural opening, EVD drainage) increases rupture risk.

q: Which grading scale uses CT findings in SAH?
why: Fisher grade uses the amount and pattern of blood on CT; WFNS and Hunt and Hess use clinical state.

q: Which aneurysm size increases rupture risk?
why: Risk factors include size over 7 mm, hypertension, smoking and seizures.

q: What is the mortality of aneurysmal SAH?
why: About 50%; only about 20% return to their previous quality of life.

q: Which post-op complication of SAH is treated with euvolaemia, nimodipine and possibly angioplasty?
why: Vasospasm (from day 3, peak days 5–7) is treated with nimodipine, euvolaemia and interventional options.

q: What is the NICE target for securing a ruptured aneurysm?
why: Secure within 24–48 hours (NICE target under 48 hours) to reduce rebleeding.

q: Which hyponatraemic condition after SAH is hypovolaemic and must NOT be fluid restricted?
why: Cerebral salt wasting causes sodium and water loss; fluid restriction would worsen vasospasm. Treat with sodium and fluid.
